utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We were dealing yesterday with Kotlina, and there was an outstanding query raised by His Honour Judge Bonomy, and I'll just conclude what I want to deal with so far as Kotlina is concerned and tidy up that question. Mr. Jelic, I asked you some questions yesterday. You'll remember that the allegations include that 17 people were killed in places described as wells by the use of explosives. May we just have a look, please, at Exhibits 54, 55, and then 57A, just to remind ourselves of what the evidence is about. The Chamber may recall this object, this picture. If I can put that on the overhead projector. It was holes in a wood, large holes in a wood in which the bodies were deposited. Do you have any record or recollection of these holes, Mr. Jelic?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No record about any holes, or these caves, rather, because I wasn't there, in the first place, with my units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Observations have been made about whether the men concerned were KLA. That's never been challenged that there was an element of KLA involved or that people who were killed included people who had a KLA interest. And if we just look at -- I think it's this exhibit, 59A. Again to remind the Chamber, the appearance of the people who were killed. Very rapidly, just so that we can make the point. They are indeed young men, a lot of them. One by -- and the next one, please. Next. And then the next one. Thank you very much. Okay. If I can have those back, please. If we can now put on the overhead projector Exhibit 1 -- or give me Exhibit 163, tab -- that's fine. Thank you very much. We can have them all back now. Exhibit 163, tab 4 -- well, tab 3 and tab 4, but, Your Honour, this deals with His Honour Judge Bonomy's point and concern. 163, tab 4, is a report of the Austrian Kosovo crime scene, and, Your Honours, without going through it in detail, if I can just put one passage on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't my concern, Mr. Nice, to hear again what the Prosecution case was. My concern was that the witness made a distinction between Kacanik and Kotlina and it wasn't clear to me what he was answering and I wanted that cleared up. I don't want a regurgitation of the Prosecution evidence on the point, because we just don't have time for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. I thought Your Honour was concerned because he said I don't understand why it's Kotlina and Kacanik, and the answer to that is clearly contained. What happened -- just lay that on the overhead projector. To settle the witness's concern, and I thought maybe Your Honour's, it doesn't matter -- it does matter, but it's the Austrians examined the scene, and this is part of what they dealt with, and if the Court will take it from me, the Austrians went to the scene, they discovered the bodies, and then they explain that it was the Swiss autopsy team that conducted the detailed examination, but they conducted the examination at Kacanik, which is five kilometres away. So that -- so that that's the reason that a Kotlina death was actually finally explored. If I could have that piece of paper back. We've dealt with that. And finally, on the question of whether these people were members of the KLA or not, in addition to the evidence that we've called where I think the witness denied KLA activity, we'll look at just one very short passage from "As Seen, As Told," which is page -- well, it appears in both books and I'll just put it on. "As Seen, As Told," page 219, so that there's no doubt about how this has always been made absolutely clear. This is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice says that the witness denied KLA activity. That's not true at all. He never denied KLA activity. On the contrary; he spoke about KLA activity in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On this -- to the extent that -- we'll just deal with that. To the extent there was any denial of activity by those who died, it's dealt with in several places, and if we just look at this passage here, we see that -- this is in "As Seen, As Told," and I'll read it to you, the material parts, in English. It deals with the fact that - at the top of the page 22 - people were allegedly killed, sets out a detailed account, sets out reservations of the OSCE on a follow-up investigation; how they found corroboration broadly of the accounts that were given, deals with the allocation of the bodies in the well, and then says: "Of the whole group of 22 men --" this is right at the foot of the page -- "11 were apparently unarmed UCK soldiers in civilian clothes, selected and taken to the area close to the 'wells' --" right at the bottom of the page -- "where they were beaten, shots (probably of an execution) were later heard, and finally there was the noise of a loud explosion ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that, Mr. Jelic, I come back to the question that I was asking you about right at the beginning. This is a quick summary of the evidence, it deals with the point you were raising about Kotlina and Kacanik, and I'm asking you, finally, having thought about it overnight, can you give any explanation for why these men, found in the wells in a place where your troops were active in the area, were dead, for the most part as a result of explosions consistent with grenade explosions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area that you mentioned, Kotlina, is about 15 kilometres away from Kacanik, not three to five kilometres. Kotlina is in the border belt, within five kilometres. I mentioned during my testimony so far that from Kotlina there were constant attacks on the in-depth security units. The units was practically engaged in weekly fighting with the terrorists from the region. Not from the village but from the region Ivaja-Kotlina-Pustenik. So that is the concentration of the terrorist forces. We had an order. I think that I presented it here, that ever since 1998 the army was banned from entering inhabited areas, particularly with heavy equipment, and we strictly observed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, do you have an answer to the question or don't you, which is whether you have an explanation as to why these men, found in wells in places where your troops were active, were dead for the most part as a result of explosions, which explosions are consistent with grenade explosions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no explanation because my units did not enter the village nor do I know of such a pit, and I've never heard of that or, rather, I never heard of it until the end of the war. It was only later, here in court, that I heard about such victims and that they are allegedly civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: General, what could conceivably have happened to these people other than that they were attacked in some way? Maybe justifiably, but all the signs are that they died through some form of attack. Now, you just know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have any information about these people, because in that period the army did not enter the village of Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it, Mr. Jelic, that you're suggesting that in an area which provided the -- well, covered the route down to the Djeneral Jankovic crossing and which was known to have KLA activists in it, you're saying that your army was simply driving up and down the road, because it wouldn't go into the villages, and being attacked, simply, by the KLA. Is that what you're really saying?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "driving up and down." Is that some kind of a stroll? I don't understand this. The units were moving along --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... saying that your army never went into the villages where it's known that there was KLA activity. Well, if you didn't go into the villages, how could the KLA ever attack you? What they were doing? We haven't got your logbooks, we haven't got the unit's records; we don't know what you're suggesting. How could the KLA attack you if you didn't go to their villages?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that five or six times before this Court I stated what KLA tactics were. You say that they're civilians. These are armed civilians that did not attack from villages but they attack along roads north-south, that is to say towards Djeneral Jankovic and Globocica. They never used villages for protection. On the contrary, since this is a highly forested area - you cannot see this on this map because it is a photocopy - the altitude is about 1.000 metres, there's lots of woods there, and it is highly inaccessible. They would walk, they would fire a few bursts of gunfire, and then, when there was gunfire response, then they would flee through the woods, probably to their homes or to their bases. We don't know from what villages they came and where they were from. We could never obtain accurate information on that, but we assumed that they were people from the neighbouring villages. As you can see, there are no such problems to the east and west, on both sides. It is all in the areas where the combat disposition of the units is, which in itself indicates that they were incessantly attacking our units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you really saying you never went to a village to try and take out the KLA, in the vernacular? You never did that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not go into any village to neutralise KLA members. As for the area of the villages, yes, but there's a world of difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's move to the next topic I was going to ask you about of the other two that I'm going to deal with very briefly. Ivaja. It's mentioned at paragraph 63(k) of the indictment, where it is said that between March and May of 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia attacked villages in Kacanik municipality and the town of Kacanik itself. This attack resulted in the destruction of houses and religious sites including but not limited to the mosques of Kotlina and Ivaja. Can we just look, please, at a couple of entries in the blue book, which is Exhibit 321. Mr. Jelic, these are records. The format is familiar to the Court, but it may not be to yourself - I'll have to read it to you in English in any event - of the OSCE mission, and this entry is for the 9th of March, so before any question of a declaration of state of emergency or war. And the representatives, the observers recorded that, "The VJ/MUP operation to clear the KLA from the Djeneral Jankovic area continues." Well, first of all, were the OSCE wrong in saying that there was a joint exercise by the VJ and the MUP to clear this area, this area leading to Djeneral Jankovic, of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Djeneral Jankovic is highly populated, and it's a big area. There was no plan for that kind of cleaning. The plan was to defend units from terrorist attacks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were down there with the MUP, and you were doing something but it wasn't to clean the area.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking about me myself, me personally, no. My units were in that area for over a year, and from the secession of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, because that is where there is a border crossing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, I'm asking about your units, not about you personally. So I'll ask the question again: Were your units there with the MUP to do something against the KLA but not to clean the area? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units were there all the time. That could be seen on the diagram here and on the decision of the federal government. There was no police at the border crossing except for Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just read on. How OSCE or KVM reported it was: "Their patrols were initially blocked from proceeding to the affected villages. MUP and VJ forces then followed their pattern of surrounding the local villages, forcing the inhabitants to flee through the use of direct and indirect fire. By mid-afternoon, houses were burning in Gajre, Ivaja, Straza, Alil Mahala. MUP units appeared intent on destroying those villages." Is there any reason to doubt the accuracy of what the OSCE recorded then, including what it recorded about Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned several villages here, practically the entire territory of the municipality. The army did not leave its own areas. It did not leave them. I don't know what patrols you mean were stopped and blocked. Are you referring to MUP patrols, because they are the official ones, or are you referring to some other patrols? I don't understand the way you phrased your question. Which patrols? Are you referring to KLA patrols?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you one more chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand whether Mr. Nice is citing a specific OSCE document, an OSCE report. I have no such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 321. The accused's memory will remind him that we've looked at this document on many occasions. It's a compilation of daily reports from the OSCE observers in the field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Jelic, if you really didn't understand what I said, I'll repeat it but I'll make it simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's now on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The OSCE report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not an OSCE document. That is from that book "As Seen, As Told." It's not a document. It's that book where all sorts of things are written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I get on with the questioning, Your Honours? This is the blue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In any event this is the document to which Mr. Nice is referring. It's on the ELMO. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll make the proposition even simpler: The OSCE observers in the field reported that MUP and VJ forces surrounded villages, forced inhabitants to flee by direct and indirect fire, and set light to houses including houses, just make it really narrow, including houses at Ivaja. Is that true? May that be true?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true at all. The army never entered the villages. It never set houses on fire, and it never expelled the population. It's our own population. Why would they expel them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would you say that there was any question of a joint operation by you and the MUP on the villages of Straza, Ivaja, Gajre, Kotlina? Any question of such a joint operation? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no joint operation. There was only fighting against terrorists when they would appear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I have the document back. We'll have another look at what is reported on the following day and then we'll be nearly done with Ivaja but not quite. You see, on the following day the same OSCE mission reported this in respect of Ivaja, that -- their reconnaissance patrol, I think number 5 -- no, forget that. The KVM escorted a UNHCR convoy in the heart of the salient. They were stopped by VJ and MUP but eventually allowed to proceed and three bodies in civilian clothes were found in Ivaja, which is totally deserted, as is Gajre. Then the observers commented that the VJ was maintaining a small garrison of soldiers and equipment, at least four BOVs and four cargo trucks, in Djeneral Jankovic. Can you account for three bodies in civilian clothes - dead bodies - in Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give an explanation for these three corpses in Ivaja because you're saying that they're in civilian clothes. Not a single terrorist was wearing any kind of uniform as a member of some army. Throughout the war and in 1998, they wore civilian clothing and they carried rifles in their hands. Most probably these three fought against the soldiers and got killed. If this is related to Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's related --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you said --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's related to Ivaja. You were asked questions by the accused about Ivaja, so presumably you knew Ivaja was going to come up. We have seen no documents showing what your troops were doing on any day, let alone the 9th and 10th. Can you account, please, for these three men being killed in Ivaja on the 9th or 10th?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they got killed, but you mentioned that the army was in the Djeneral Jankovic garrison. So it's not by accident that I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the witness's other microphone please be turned on. We have difficulty hearing him when he's talking to Mr. Nice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher could very kindly turn on -- thank you. And that for the witness, that for the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just look at this document, please. It's coming to you in B/C/S, and we'll put the English version on the overhead projector. Now, this is dated the 9th of March, and this is what it says: It says: "Starting at 0530 on the 8th of March ... members of the Urosevac SUP and Gnjilane SUP special police units, together with members of the VJ, launched an operation to clear the villages of Straza, Ivaja, Gajre and Kotlina, Kacanik municipality, of the terrorist gangs which have carried out terrorist operations in this area with attacks on members ..." and so on. So what do you say about this document? You've denied the accuracy -- the suggestion that there was any joint operation, so what do you say about this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to read the document first in order to say anything about it. Not for a single moment did I deny that there was a joint struggle against terrorism. You said before this that the army entered villages together with the police in order to expel the population. That's not the same thing. This is the area where the units were. This is where the combat disposition of the units was, and I explained that there were units for the fight against terrorism of battalion size or artillery battalion size. If there was an attack on the army of Yugoslavia, we took measures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me remind you of a question and answer that happened a couple of minutes ago. I said to you in these terms: "Was there any question of a joint operation by you and the MUP on the villages of Straza, Ivaja, Gajre? Any suggestion of a joint operation?" Your answer: "There was no joint operation. There was only fighting against terrorists when they would appear." On a simple reading, Mr. Jelic, your answers would appear to be inconsistent. Now, why did you say the first thing and now why have you changed your mind? Is it because you've been caught by that document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. I abide by what I said the first time, but you didn't say here what you said before, that there were expulsions and cleansing of the terrain. You left this out on purpose to prove that we did what you're trying to prove.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Read your entire question. You have it in the transcript and you'll see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, just listen to the questions and answer them. Look at this paragraph. It makes it clear that there was a joint operation to -- with the MUP to clear the villages. Now, ten or 15 minutes ago you were saying you never went into the villages. Well, which is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never did the army enter villages. I repeat again: Never did the army enter the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us -- tell us what you did in this joint operation that you didn't remember five minutes ago. What was your part in the joint operation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered it very well five minutes ago and five days ago, and now I remember it very well several years later. That's what you say. When the terrorists turned up, the task of the army was to block them. If they were in inhabited places, they left them to the MUP. If they were out in the open, there was a fight to the death.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there is a misunderstanding here. General Jelic is a professional soldier --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Normally when the accused starts doing this he's trying to rehearse the witness and my questions are entirely clear and the accused should not be allowed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you're making a comment, I'll not allow it. If you have an objection to make, then you can make it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to comment but to help understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, it's not for you. You can raise that in re-examination. It's not for you to help us to understand. You can ask the question in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm helping you to understand what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but you're not giving evidence. You're not in the box. You don't understand these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic - and I'm going to move on to my last area in a second - but what the OSCE records about you working together with the MUP, softening up the villages by attacking them, letting the MUP go in and do whatever they had to do, is completely accurate, isn't it? This is -- and remember, this is --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army did not attack villages. That's not correct. Wherever members of the KLA turned up, they blocked those areas. It says here in the village of Ivaja. You didn't let me read it through to the end. Every document has to be analysed and yet you're asking me to comment on it before I've had a chance to do that. Look what it says about the village of Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading much too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This confirms what I said previously. In principle, that's what was done in each inhabited place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means read it. It says in the bottom paragraph on the screen --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- "In the village of Ivaja, the PJPs smashed a large group of terrorists and destroyed the staff of the so-called KLA 162nd Brigade. In the process, a large amount of mines and explosives, hand-held rocket launchers," and so on was captured. And if we could have it a little higher up, please. Now, this was a joint -- let's see how it goes on: "A large amount of medical material was also seized and destroyed, and documentation indicating the organisation of the terrorist groups and their operations were seized too. The operation to clear the terrorist groups in these villages was completed at 1730 ..." Now, I'm not in a position one way or another to make an assertion about the accuracy of how the conduct -- how the combat in the village occurred and how people died, but it makes it clear that the operation was concluded. Now, this was a joint operation. So you, as one of the parties to the joint operation, will have kept a record of what happened. Why when I asked you not so long ago if you had no -- if you had any explanation for how three people were killed in Ivaja, why didn't you tell us it was the result, one way or the other, of a joint operation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that three persons were killed there. I don't know when, at what time they were killed. You can say any time, but without a document I cannot recall because six years have elapsed. It's absurd for someone to remember details on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course without a document you can't recall a thing. Do you not think it's an insult to intelligence, Mr. Jelic, to have come to this court without making any effort to look at any one of the range of contemporaneous documents that existed? Do you not think that's an insult to intelligence?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why it would be an insult. What documents are you referring to? If I don't have the documents I cannot comment on them nor can I evaluate them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, just a few minutes ago you said that you remember this whole matter and the answers you gave five minutes ago, "and I remember the incident well five years ago," you used the expression. And you were asked some time ago if you could explain why there would be three bodies in Ivaja, and you put the shutters up completely to that. You didn't even suggest to us, "Well, maybe it was because of a police action that I know was going on between the 8th and 10th of March." Now, why is it you do that? Why don't you try to assist the Bench to get to the truth of these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot help this Chamber, nor can I give general responses. I said that I remembered the questions that were put to me and my responses and the general content of the documents, but where someone was killed and under what conditions, it would be absurd for somebody to recall that without looking at a document in that entire situation. You're now trying to discuss this particular area, and before that you discussed the cleansing of Djeneral Jankovic and the joint operation of the police and army. It's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, the question was: "Tell us what you did in this joint operation that you didn't remember five minutes ago. What was your part in the joint operation?" And the answer was, "I remembered it very well five minutes ago and five days ago, and now I remember it very well several years later." Now, do you want to take that answer back now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't want to take it back. The army was securing its flanks and wings from the places where the terrorists were emerging, and it was fighting the terrorists. That was the army's main task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move on to the last topic, which I can deal with very briefly, just confirm this: To your knowledge, are you the only person from your brigade who is coming here to give evidence on behalf of this accused?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that by coming here without any contemporaneous records yourself and just giving generalised answers, if we don't get hold of the records, we'll never be able to find from anyone else what it is said your troops were doing on, for example, the 9th and 10th of March of 1999; is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't think that's for the witness to answer. Move on, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. The Court will want to know that the document we were looking at was Defence Exhibit 312, tab 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Janicevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we move now to the third area I'll deal with, very briefly. Stagovo, once again you dealt with in evidence yourself, we can see where it is on the map there, for the assistance of the Trial Chamber. What's said about Stagovo in the indictment is at 63(k)(ii) and 66(l)(iii). I'll deal just with 66(l)(iii). "On or about the 21st of May of 1999, the village of Stagovo, or Stagove, was surrounded by the forces of the FRY and Serbia. The population tried to escape towards the mountains east of the village. During the action, at least 12 persons were killed. Most of the village was looted and burnt down." What do you know about this? Let me help you with the date so that you can give us your best recollection. 21st of May of 1999.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the village of Stagovo is a case in point because, from the general area of the village, not the village itself, there were constant attacks towards Kamena Glava and towards our positions. The attacks took place by night, and on three or four occasions the terrorists entered a minefield. The troops could not abandon their artillery pieces to enter into the village. The troops did not enter the village of Stagovo, they only fought the terrorists in the area to the north of the village. There was no joint operation and no entry into the village of Stagovo. If defence is to be considered an operation, then, yes, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the evidence before the Court about Stagovo includes that on that particular day VJ soldiers were seen in the area by a witness, Dashi. People retreated. Mortars and gunfire could be heard, and after Serb forces left, bodies were found in the village. Can you please explain how bodies -- how people came to be killed in that village?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this unit does not have mortars. It has anti-army artillery. How those people lost their lives, I really don't know. I can only assume that they participated in fighting. The army was there, but they could have been seen between Stari Kacanik and Stagovo, where their positions were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these people who were fighting may have lost their lives, and as I think you told us, when there's a loss of life there has to be a record made, so somewhere in the army's record there will be a record of how these people lost their lives, will there? In general or specific terms there will be some kind of record?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In clearing up the terrain, whenever corpses were found, any of -- any provenance - because there was crime there as well - any body that was found was dealt with in the way prescribed by law and according to international law, which means that every body was collected, humanely buried, the grave was marked, and the documentation was handed over to the local authorities, in this case in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can be confident, can we, that the material handed over in respect of the Stagovo killings to the authorities in Kacanik will reveal how, in all probability, those who died were armed and engaged in battle at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say exactly what is contained in those documents, first of all. Secondly, it depends on who found them. If they were found by the MUP or the army, there would have been an investigating judge. They would have had to be humanely buried, the graves marked, and there had to be proper documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the Court's assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll just lay this on the overhead projector. This is part of Exhibit 163, tab 11. It's in English but I can read what's material to you. It comes from the Swiss forensic report, and their investigation happened on the 24th to the 25th of September of 1999 where they dealt with a communal grave in Stagovo. And you can see, because this much will be apparent to you, that included in those killed were a 74-year-old woman, a 7-year-old boy, a woman born in 1954, therefore 45 at the time, a woman born in 1916, another woman born in 1943. Would you care to help us from your memory, Mr. Jelic, with how any operation of which you were a party in this place killed those people? Because their -- everyone who has a remaining interest in them would like to know. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say that the army took part in an operation. I have repeated several times that the army did not participate in any operation or enter the village of Stagovo. As for the death of these people, I have no reason to doubt that they were actually killed, but I don't know where. I don't know who gave this information. I can doubt it. Maybe they died of natural causes. I don't know what this is about. Please remember that elderly people might have died of natural causes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was gunshot and knife wounds, Your Honours, by which they were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just last point on Stagovo and then I'll be done apart from two other questions. Apart from the evidence we've laid before the Court, another collection of material deals with the same point, and since it's -- page 221 on the overhead projector. Bottom left-hand corner of that page, please. And it deals with: "On the 30th of April, Stagovo east of highway 2 and just below Stari Kacanik, beside the main railway line, was shelled. Police took up positions around the village but didn't enter it," and there was fighting. Then it says this: "In May the UCK had a 'stronghold' close to the village, and on the 21st of May Stagovo was attacked again. VJ and police shelled the village from a distance and the villages -- villagers started to flee towards the mountains." Now, this specifically identifies the VJ. Do you have any recollection of what they did on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're confirming what I just said; the army was fighting the terrorists. Terrorists were in the village of Stagovo. When you say "village," you're probably referring to the centre of the village, but you shoot at the army from the centre of the village. Wherever there were terrorists, the army fought them fiercely. The village of Stagovo -- I don't really understand this in translation. You say the MUP was searching the village of Stagovo, chasing this gang that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I have to express concern that, being pushed for time as you are, you're resorting in cross-examination to material which is not even part of the evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This book is an exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've just said it is a collection of material which you haven't so far presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I said that, I didn't mean to say that. This is material that is indeed in the case, and indeed it's very much part of the evidence, and I'm sorry about that. But you see, the reason I mention it is for this, and this is the last reason, something I want the witness's assistance with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This says specifically -- and I've just now lost my place, but -- there we are. This says that the killings were done by paramilitaries. We can see it there. It says -- deals with the interviews, Mr. Jelic, describes how people, including women and paralysed grandmother, were executed by paramilitaries and how houses were set on fire. Do your recollections of what you the military were doing with the police include recollections that paramilitaries were involved as well? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're lying, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So these people who give an account of the death of women and children are either -- is there any chance, do you think, from uniforms, that the military might be confused for paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you put it back on the ELMO for me. Mr. Nice, where is the passage that you read saying that the village was shelled from a distance -- from a distance?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "... on the 21st of May Stagovo was attacked again. VJ and police shelled --" top right-hand corner "-- the village from a distance, and the villagers started to flee towards the mountains."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to ask the general something about that, because he has said consistently that the army never entered the villages. Is this consistent with what you're saying, that the shelling took place from a distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The army never attacks villages or enters villages. We are not authorised to search villages. If from an inhabited, a built-up area, a fortification is created, the army breaks it up. Everything else, every other populated area is left to the MUP, which fights the terrorists in built-up areas, searches houses and does whatever they're authorised to do. In this case there was a group of terrorists near Stagovo. If the army did not respond to that, it would not have been carrying out its task. As for the last question, how can a person, an ordinary citizen, know enough to talk about paramilitaries in some distant, faraway village? Please bear in mind the level of education of these people. Bear in mind their background and their culture. When they see a person in uniform, they call him either a policeman or a soldier. They don't use the term "paramilitary." This is absurd. You're giving a list, and if you tell me of one single soldier of mine who is said to be a paramilitary, and I will take responsibility for everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the general strategy is that the army operated from a distance and the MUP would enter the villages to deal with the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's the general principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General. General, do you exclude the possibility that there exists a person or persons who were armed separate from military or police, be it legal or illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't exclude that possibility. There may have been criminal gangs, just as there might be in peacetime. Under ordinary conditions there are criminals, and their numbers may have increased. They may have been linked together more under conditions of wartime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Some ordinary people call them paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our language, I do apologise, this is a term introduced recently. I would call it an imported term. You talk either of rebels or renegades or of policemen or soldiers. As for the term "paramilitary," it's something that has been imposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to organised things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And turning back to Stagovo, is it true that the army shelled the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army did not shell the village. The terrorist group to the north of Stagovo pushed back by the police -- the MUP had been attacked in Kacanik previously and pushed them back, and they attempted to cross the positions of the anti-armour detachment, and that's where the armoured forces were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you saying that army never shelled at any point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They never shelled the village. They never shelled the village itself. I would have had a report had it been done. There was a report that there was fighting above Stagovo and that they even entered a minefield, probably attempting to approach the positions or attempting to flee the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My question was wrong. The army shelled the firing point. That's correct, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question, which in a sense follows on from His Honour Judge Kwon's, is this: You say that -- you said to me that there was no question of your soldiers being mistaken for people described as paramilitaries. It's right, isn't it, certainly that in the 26th of March order you were commanding not only the army but also armed non-Siptar people. That would be Serbs who had been provided with arms. Now, could such people be, in your judgement, confused by those using the term "paramilitaries"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, how people could have used different expressions is something that I cannot answer, and probably no one can answer what somebody would have said for those men then. As for what it says in that document that you refer to, in addition to the army of Yugoslavia, we had the Ministry of Defence which armed people in order to protect vital facilities, namely post offices, banks, telephone exchanges, transformer stations, and other key facilities that are within the area of responsibility. All these people who were organised, who were placed under the command either of the ministry or the army or the MUP cannot be called paramilitaries because it's not that they're doing something apart from the army. They are, within the scope of their activities, soldiers too, doing a certain job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, you say the general strategy was that the army would operate from a distance while the police would go into the villages to deal with the rebels or whatever you call them. Was the reason for that merely tactical or -- or were there constitutional, legal reasons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, when terrorist groups appear in an open space, then it is very clear and simple. Then they are surrounded and destroyed. However, if these groups flee into inhabited areas, then the military blocks the village from the side where they are and the MUP enters the village, searches the buildings, and engages in fighting in built-up areas. The army does not enter the village, and the army does not fire because then you would be firing at random. You don't have a front. You don't have an army in front of you. These were usually groups of ten or 15, up to 50 people at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one other question. How old is the usage of the term "paramilitary" in your country? You said it was of just recent usage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit that this term "paramilitary" has been used, say, from the 1990s onwards. Unfortunately, these are terms that came into being during the disintegration of Yugoslavia when certain political parties, not only in Serbia but throughout Yugoslavia, used them. All of them used them for their own interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finished on those three topics, Your Honours, yes. And I was going to ask two other questions of a general nature. They are these, with the Court's leave:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any records that you can remember, point us to that detail the taking of any prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this question is for me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- then prisoners of war are usually recorded by the MUP and the security organs, if there are any. I had no prisoners of war, nor did we have any records. There were people who would be detained in custody for a day or two, as you saw from the report of the corps commander, but we did not have any prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Obilic electric plant in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. As far as I know, there are no electric plants in Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I wish to ask this witness. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make one point, please, in private session? I'll explain my position, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is no electric plant in Pristina. Like in Prizren, in Pristina there is no electric plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is there any reason why the transcript of the exchanges that have just taken place should remain confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why? Let's -- too much is assumed here by the Prosecution that when they make these applications. In my submission, absolutely nothing in what was said that remotely impinges upon the interests of justice in this case. No names are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not the interests of justice; security.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Where? It's simply not identified in any way. The short answer is given, yes, without any explanation. It may well be a knee-jerk reaction by Mr. Nice not getting his way on something. In our submission, no details were given and the Prosecution should identify what sensitivities there were about the matters in closed session, and point to how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, justify it. I think Mr. Kay is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the suggestion of knee-jerk reaction is, if I may say so, unhelpful. Of course I thought about this matter in considerable detail, and if you would be good enough -- do you have the facility to wind back the LiveNote? Page 31, lines 12 to 14, and then if you go back to the first part, to line -- lines 22 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this in private session or not now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in public session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We should be in private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic. Let's not have an unnecessary comment. It's your time to re-examine, and I want to tell you that -- or to remind you about the purposes of re-examination. You need not be overly long. Just concentrate on the issues in respect of which you think the witness needs some kind of rehabilitation. Please begin. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, was there a tank in operation in Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single tank was operating in Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does anybody there have tanks except for you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; just my brigade, my tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you assert with 100 per cent certainty that a tank was not firing?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert with 100 per cent certainty that on the 15th a tank was not firing. I'm not talking about the 17th, 18th or 19th. I'm only talking about the 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could it happen that a tank would be operating and that you would not know about it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is it absolutely impossible?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible because of the command and because of the explosion that could be heard and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can hear the difficulty the interpreter is having. You must observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the tank not shell to the direction of Belince on 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fire was not open -- I'm sorry. Fire was not opened in the direction of Belince, hardly ever. The PAM and the Praga fired in the direction of the Belince, that is to say south of Belince, that's where fire was opened from at the army, that elevation without a name, the one that I showed you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even then, when fire was opened, a tank was not used?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A tank was not used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell me what PAM is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An anti-aircraft machine-gun, but that is an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The calibre is 12.7 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you're a professional soldier. What does the word "operation" mean from a military point of view?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operation means something that is done at highest level; at corps level or even larger units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can any of the activities that were conducted there be called an operation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single one of these activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So why are you using the word "operation"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operation denotes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you why are you using the word "operation" when you're answering Mr. Nice's questions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An operation means an activity aimed at taking care of a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This activity that you described, is that the only activity? So if a terrorist group jeopardises a unit by opening fire, then you open fire at that group.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but that's not an operation. This is combat activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you have joint combat activities with the MUP regarding some group, some terrorist groups in that area, and when? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for individual groups, we never had plans because we never knew and we could not assess when things would happen. At the moment when things would happen, the army would carry out a blockade and the MUP would search the inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It is the terrorists who are attacking who are dictating when attacks will take place?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. And, Mr. Milosevic, do not forget one thing: This map and the order we have encompasses everything. There are no additional orders. It regulates everything. Unfortunately, we haven't gone through it completely here, but everything is stated there; how fighting is conducted and against who. If you can, look at the last points, who is engaged in anti-terrorist action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, open the order now and please read what it says. It's very important for you, General, to explain that, because this is probably the only place in the world where they are trying to say that it is a crime when terrorists get killed when fighting against an army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have an exact reference of what will be read out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreter is asking for a precise reference --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Tab number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- reading from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it now. It's in one of the tabs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it. It's in tab 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tab 19. That is the order that was written by the witness, General Jelic. So, General, we are not going to go through this order. We did not do it during the examination-in-chief either, but just in relation to this explanation that was provided to you during the cross-examination, fighting against terrorists and everything. So what did you write here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 8, paragraph 8.3, what the focus of the activity will be. "During sabotage and terrorist operations, security support must be focussed on detecting, monitoring, crushing and destroying DTG, sabotage and terrorist groups, and insurgent forces in the brigade's zone of responsibility. "a), for combat against DTG, special forces and insurgent forces attacking military facilities and housing facilities of brigade members. The military police is to be primarily engaged in these tasks."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say, "Engaged 2 VP"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd platoon of the military police. That is there for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about engaging a platoon of the military police?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it important to see - how should I put this? - how big the unit that you're engaging for this is.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're engaging a platoon of the military police to react if this happens?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's that. In view of the specific nature of the activity involved, and they are trained and equipped to fight against smaller terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers are in this platoon?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 45 to 50 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what does it say here? The 1st Platoon of the military police shall act as reserve?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is in accordance with my order. So these are the exact tasks, who was doing what in which area. But what is important is subparagraph A, the one that I referred to. Then there is traffic control and so on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no need to explain this any further. So what is stated here in your order is that which actually covers your reaction, your intention, and the point of this kind of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's it. These are units that are trained and ready to take momentary action against the terrorists. The terrorists are not engaged in frontal fighting. They attack, they carry out sabotage, and they try to run away as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It was stated here that you do not know how to answer the question what your units were doing on the 9th and 10th of March.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I know what my units were doing, Mr. Milosevic. We were engaged in fighting in this area all the time. I will give you an example. On the 9th of March there was an attack on Combat Group 3. That is in the area of Globocica. That's when two of our soldiers got wounded. They lost their legs. I know what my losses were but I don't know about the terrorist losses because they certainly got their casualties out, their wounded and dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've dealt with that as a question. It was said here -- Mr. Robinson asked you whether your strategy was to fight from a distance and for the police to enter certain areas. What kind of strategy is this, General? Let me understand, because I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strategy is a broad notion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to tell us what a strategy is, but in what sense did you use the word strategy? That is what I would like to have explained.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is a terrorist group in any area and they mostly appeared in open areas vis-a-vis the army, the army immediately reacts with the forces that are there for anti-terrorist fighting. If the terrorists flee into inhabited areas, regardless of whether they are from these inhabited areas or not, the army blocks that region where the -- they came. North, south, east, west; it doesn't matter. They immediately report to the MUP organs, they inform them about this. Then the MUP comes in and then they search or, rather, control the houses, the facilities there, whatever was used. Perhaps it was a socially owned facility or a private house or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that, as a rule, the army does not enter villages.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule and also in accordance with the order of the chief of General Staff from 1998, we were forbidden from doing that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, could you repeat your question. The interpreters couldn't follow you because both of you spoke too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And at the same time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And please speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall bear that in mind, Mr. Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this some kind of strategy or is there an order from top levels that the army cannot enter villages?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comes from the chief of General Staff, this order, and it went all the way to battalion commanders that the army cannot enter populated areas to engage in fighting, that fighting can be engaged in only outside populated areas and that populated areas can only be blocked. And also in that order it says that they cannot use heavy equipment, especially for fighting in built-up areas, in order not to have housing facilities destroyed and in order to prevent civilians from being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In response to Mr. Robinson's question, you said that you shelled from a distance. Now, could you explain this, please. What was it that you were shelling from a distance? What was it that you were shelling from a distance? Explain what you said. I'm not asking you a different question, I'm asking you what he asked you. You said, yes, we were firing from a distance. What were you shelling from a distance?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stagovo, where a terrorist group was, as the Prosecutor said here, was above Stagovo. And the army automatically responded to the gunfire of that terrorist group. They used artillery pieces to fire at them, and mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a moment. Were you shelling Stagovo from a distance?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, a group --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute, General. You have to bear in mind what you're doing, what you're saying by way of response. If Judge Robinson asked you whether you were shelling Stagovo from a distance, you are shelling a village from a distance.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am saying --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a combat group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a minute, I'm not interested in your combat group. I'm interested in whether your combat group was firing at a village from a distance.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a village but the area where the combat group was. Not the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that you were firing at?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The terrorists who were expelled from Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you firing at? Leave the history aside. What were you firing at?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrorists, military objectives, KLA, armed people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north of Stagovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much to the north?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 400 to 500 metres, right by our combat positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And where were you firing from at them?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below old Kacanik. You have this here on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Show it on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him show it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't hear. We didn't hear you, General. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again I'm repeating it. This is where the unit took up its positions. This is the village of Stagovo, right here, and the group that appeared was here, to the east of this anti-armour detachment here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And that, you say, is 400 metres to the north of Stagovo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. 400 metres east of the combat position. 400 or 500 metres. If you can see, it's in this forested area, on the rim of the forest, that is. There is an elevation here 400, 500 metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll have to adjourn now for 20 minutes. We'll take the break. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the term "shelling" is often used here. I assume this refers to targeting something with artillery weapons. Is that how you understand the term?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Literally translated, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your units which had artillery weapons -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever shell any village at all?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single village was shelled by a single unit. The units were not allowed to do this. As I've already said, they had orders from the superior command, and my own order and these orders were strictly complied with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. When firing from artillery pieces, does there have to be a clear target or just a general target?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The target, first of all, has to be visible with all the measurements, the distance, the size, the resistance of the target, and on this basis the kind of weapon is chosen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could have been and what was the target of your artillery in any situation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artillery weapons and tanks can only be used to target facilities such as buildings made of stone or brick or concrete, and possibly other facilities which can be misused for military purposes, such as houses of worship even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when are all these buildings targets for the army? Let's say a house or any other kind of building or facility. When does it become a target?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all you have to do reconnaissance and know what was in the house, whether there are armed terrorists there, whether they are opening fire on members of the army of Yugoslavia, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Does that mean that the target can only be a building from which fire is opened or any building?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A building that is fired from and its surrounding area, that is a target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Was there ever a case in your experience when fire was opened on an unclear target; a village, for example?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Fire was never opened at random. It was opened primarily in open areas from smaller calibre weapons, such as mortars, in various areas of broken terrain where the terrorists were fleeing or hiding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go back to Kotlina. Mr. Nice read from the book "As Seen, As Told" a letter from some people from Kotlina, as he said. Would you please put on the ELMO these photographs. I wish to mention that these are photographs from an on-site investigation of the 24th of March, as is evident from the accompanying report in the text. There are several houses visible here.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's one in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see three houses here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, three in the top part and at least two in the bottom part.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have any of these houses been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single one. They're even in excellent condition. You can see there are windows, doors, even a satellite dish. It's not a ruin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed and look at the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this first photograph shows whole houses, complete houses. There are three here, and they are in good order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the exhibit number of this? It may be part of Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is part of Stevanovic's exhibit. I don't have the tab number with me here. I do now. It's tab 212.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go on looking at the photographs, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The third house you can see the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You don't have to explain in detail. It says here that this was the KLA staff. Does it say that underneath in the caption?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "The headquarters of the so-called KLA in the village of Kotlina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed to look at the next photograph. What is visible here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first photograph shows a room from the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please move on.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you can see equipment, or you can seen furniture, rather. You can see a stove, a TV set.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Will you turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see some weapons and equipment here in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please proceed. Move on.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see weapons and equipment here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So all this shows the equipment and weapons found.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is all in Kotlina, photo documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... rising from. I've made it clear on several occasions throughout the case that there's a presence of KLA here and that's one of the reasons I reminded you what was on "As Seen, As Told." So, I mean, if he wants to spend the time in this way, it's a matter for him, but it seems rather a waste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And it was not the witness who conducted this investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Move on to another matter, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I only wish to ask him as there are photographs here of Mr. Nice's constantly referring to as wells. However, these are not wells but shelters. You can see there are ladders there, that there's no water in those wells. He kept asking the witness what he knew about wells. He couldn't know anything about wells because there were no wells. These were actually dugouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have that in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We won't proceed then. On the photographs you can also see terrorists who lost their lives, with weapons, next to the shelters. You've had a chance to see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you were asked how somebody could be killed by a hand grenade in such close fighting. Is both -- are the weapons used, both firearms and hand grenades?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, hand grenades actually are weapons used in close combat, and they're used primarily for defence. It can also be an offensive weapon, but as a rule they're used for defence, and you can throw it some 30 to 50 metres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the suggestion that the three -- or that some of the victims were killed by close combat activity in which grenades were used? Is that the proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an on-site investigation, and this is the photographic documentation of what was found. The on-site investigation was carried out on the same day as the anti-terrorist action. This is the forensic documentation from the on-site investigation. I don't have the entire report with me, but a group of terrorists was killed in the village of Kotlina, and they had two dugouts which resembled wells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no point in these questions unless the witness can then tell us who might have been involved in the close combat confrontation. Now, what does the witness know about that? What do you know about the use of grenades in close contact combat in Kotlina? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably hand grenades were used for direct defence. They're thrown by hand, and you can't throw them further away than 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But who would be using them for defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Primarily the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So they killed themselves, is your theory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For defence. For offence they're used by the MUP and the army. There are two uses for hand grenades: In attack it's an offensive use, and in defence it's a defensive use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the army weren't there. They weren't involved. So who would be using the grenades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a built-up area, only the MUP and the terrorists could have used them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to the next topic. At the outset, Mr. Nice showed you a telegram sent by you, dating from 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have received a copy. I don't know whether the witness can be given a copy of the telegram presented by Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let that be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have this before you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have to look at both pages because I'm not going to be asking about details, just a general question. Would you please read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's about the command of the Pristina Corps, to whom it's addressed. "Pursuant to your telegram number --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number don't matter.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- of the 26th of July, 1994, I hereby submit the requested data."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
