utterances.text: So does it say you're sending them the information they asked for?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this imply that their telegram that you referred to is a telegram requesting information?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It sounds a bit like a leading question coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Does it imply ..." You're leading, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can I be leading? It says here, "Pursuant to your telegram number so-and-so of the 26th ..." That's what it says here. "... we hereby submit the data requested." Does this imply that in a telegram number such-and-such there is a request for information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They requested information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's not a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is a leading question. You've given him the answer. You may have asked him what it implied, you're perfectly entitled to do that, but you're not entitled to say to him, Did this imply X, Y, and Z. That's a leading question. After four years, one would have thought you would have got to grips with the idea of leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've been through this so many times. It's bordering on being abusive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly wonder why Mr. Nice raised this issue. You should have said that to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice put a question to you in connection with this map showing the disposition of the 243rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you explained that it was part of an order from the command of the Pristina Corps and that this was an excerpt pertaining to your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the heading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he asked you whether all your units had been entered in the map, and they were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he asked you why the other units had not been entered into the map. Could you please clarify your answer. Your response was that in your extract your disposition is shown in detail whereas the disposition of other units is shown only in general, and what does that actually mean? The 549th Brigade is not depicted in detail but only in general. What does that actually mean?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is probably specific terminology and not quite clear, so I will clarify. This kind of map is also accompanied by a written order, so a decision is entered into the map. The map for the entire corps is not sent to every unit because it would be too large. Each unit is provided with an extract pertaining to them, and they see who is in front of them, who is behind them, and who their neighbours are and what their fundamental tasks are. That's why the 549th is depicted here with only part of its units, only so that we would know they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your task is depicted in detail, and you're also provided with information as to who is your neighbour.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 549th and the 175th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were asked what some of the symbols on the map mean. The map which was shown - I don't have it here, Mr. Nice produced some sort of map - and you said that something is indicated in blue. Can you clarify what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, on this map, everything that is in red refers to our forces, the forces of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blue depicts the enemy, according to our rules of combat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that apart from my brigade, which is marked in red, and our neighbours, there are also blue markings. These are units grouped on the border of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. These are the brigades of the Siptar terrorist forces - there are five of them - and a tactical group comprising one armoured brigade, two mechanised brigades.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose brigades?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The multi-national forces in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: NATO?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a NATO brigade. There was one in Tetovo, more to the south; there was another brigade near Skopje; and there was one in Titov Veles. The Dutch brigade, the assault brigade, was at the airport in Petrovac, and 40 or 50 helicopters were stationed at the airport. They are depicted, this Tactical Group, and their intention was to enter the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The main axis is shown on the map here. It's Debelbel-Kacanik. That's where the main forces were to go on this Kosovo axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you explain this, General: What is depicted in blue, those forces are not there, it's only the assumed direction of their breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, their goal, their target in phases 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I hope we've clarified the map now. Mr. Nice gave you a document here, a document of yours, the commander of the 243rd Brigade. Let me just have a look. The 8th of August, 1998. The 8th of August, 1998. Have you got that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 933.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to quote what Mr. Nice quoted. I'm going to quote the end of the first paragraph. Look at what it says: "The combat equipment of the army of Yugoslavia." What does it say there? Can you read it out?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is your report. It is signed by Krsman Jelic. On page 1, the one-but-last paragraph before number 2, before paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The combat equipment of the army of Yugoslavia is engaged according to all --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let us see the English text on the ELMO. It should be lower down, lower down. Lower down. Here it is: "VJ hardware was used in full accordance with ..." So read it out.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "VJ hardware was used in full accordance with the rules of combat. It was fired only in cases of extreme necessity --" it's very hard to read this -- "at shelters, routes, bunkers and fortified elements of the Siptar terrorists."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So only at fortified elements of the Siptar terrorists.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For this kind of action, General, was it necessary to proclaim a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. A state of emergency is proclaimed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm just asking you about this particular thing.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of General Staff and the corps commander issues orders --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a unit is attacked, then we report to our superior command what was done and what was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it say on page 3?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean: "Members of the MUP and the army of Yugoslavia treated the civilian population properly, as well as their property, without looting or crime. And in individual situations, women and children got help in clothing and food."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And towards the end, it says that a tank was hit on the 25th of July and that a soldier was wounded. And on the 26th of July, another tank was hit, killing two members of the unit and wounding two more.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. A major was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether this tank that was hit, killing two members of the unit and wounding two more and on the following day, was that a consequence of the behaviour of the civilian population towards you or the consequence of a terrorist attack?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these consequences suffered by the military, and as you see here, the terrorist organisation was very well organised, armed, and equipped, and they could destroy or, rather, damage this major kind of equipment, and it's only Armbrust hand-held rocket launchers that could inflict that kind of harm. He could wear civilian clothing and lie in the grass and fire from that kind of rocket launcher, and once he gets up, he's a civilian again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. We're just briefly going to deal with tab 17. Mr. Nice kept pointing out that these reports of yours are marked "strictly confidential." Have you heard me, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, in this binder, is there a single report of yours that is not marked "Strictly confidential"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, all documents in my binder are marked as strictly confidential. I think that only one was just "confidential." The rest are "strictly confidential."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the regular regimen of providing military reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all confidential. I was only interested in knowing whether we had the incoming documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to your question, may I say that the system of strictly confidential is classified according to the level of confidentiality of the document concerned. "Strictly confidential" is the highest level of confidentiality so that the documents would not go where they're not supposed to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are most military documents categorised as such?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are categorised in different ways. There is "internal," "confidential," and "strictly confidential," and the highest level of confidentiality is "state secret."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the level of confidentiality according to the rules and appropriate acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your reports here are mostly strictly confidential.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because that is how the superior command defined them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice said there is nothing here about Racak, and it says here that on the 15th the forces of the MUP blocked, and so on and so forth. Is that everything that you have on Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is only thing that I had and that I sent to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seen it to the corps command, and the corps command further on, probably to the army command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this report show on page 2 what you testified about? It says from the area, the region of the village of Belince. I think you explained very nicely what the village is and what the area is.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say to the south about 700 metres. Is that 700 metres to the south of the village of Belince?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Fire was opened from a Browning 12.7 millimetre and a mortar 82 millimetres on the combat deployment of the combat group, and after fire was returned from a Praga and a 12.7 PAM, after firing back at the sector south of Belince the shooting stopped. The operations end there after about two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you testified about and which is contained in your report?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice then -- a daily operative report, which the 1st administration of the General Staff provides every day. Do you see how many pages it has, this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit 934.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see how many pages it has, this entire daily operative report?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's three pages here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three pages.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Three pages covering the entire army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it include the navy too?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The state -- the situation on the state border?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also regarding foreign forces?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph 5, important events, the situation in the territory, then logistical support, cooperation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what pertains to the 3rd Army here? That is one paragraph -- two paragraphs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right; two paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And in the first paragraph there's reference to Dara Glava and the fire opened there. Mr. Nice quoted the second paragraph to you. Can you please read out the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in English. Further down. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 24th of January, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. The 3rd Army, second paragraph. Do you see where it says 3rd Army, and then the second paragraph there. You see the 3rd Army? It's at the bottom of the second page. There's a total of three pages. Before the logistical support.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm sorry. It's not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 2 you have logistical support, towards the bottom of the page, and then above it you have three paragraphs that pertain to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Read out the middle paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "During the tactical exercise --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said the middle one. I'm not interested in this. He didn't quote it either. The middle paragraph, "Some of the forces ..." Can you see this?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Some of the forces of BG-243-1 were deployed to block the village of Racak --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Municipality of Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "-- municipality of Stimlje ..."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stop there now. Are those the forces that we explained here in detail that were here from April the previous year?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the forces that were checked by the verifiers when they came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we had exhibits about that too. They came and they checked them. Did those forces go anywhere to a blockade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't go anywhere. They simply took up positions in their own area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they did not go into a blockade, but the anti-terrorist action is taking place in their neighbourhood and that is why they are the blockade of that particular axis. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. On the northern side, practically by their very existence they are a blockade. Otherwise, they did not set out in order to carry out a blockade. The Prosecutor asked about the same thing on a map, and he asked me whether it was a blockade. From a certain point of view, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You've just said that by their very existence. They existed there from April 1998?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They didn't move anywhere?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't move anywhere except when they would take up positions in their own area, within that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And now tell me, what does it say here further on, in the next line? Of course it has to do with Racak, and then it says, "Where --" Read it out.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... where members of the MUP conducted an action against Siptar terrorists who had killed a MUP member."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What does it say? Who was carrying out this action in Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that the MUP members were carrying it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So it was the MUP members that were carrying that out. That's what it says in the operative report as well.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have that in the corps too. If you've got that, then you can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no denying that. But I just wanted to see this since it does say here that it was the members of the MUP who were carrying this out. Now, Mr. Nice gave you D395. I jotted that down. A handwritten diary of your commander of combat group Cafa Dulje.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it please be given to the witness. 395.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I wrote down was 395. It was probably misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have the second page? What is this? It says Dragan Todorovic signed it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's a lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the commander of that combat group of yours which, in accordance with the agreement reached with the OSCE, was in that area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was acting on behalf of Lieutenant Colonel Djordjevic who was the commander of the group, so at that time he was the commander of that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It says there that indeed that is a contemporaneous document from that date, the 15th.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is the original.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice obtained it, as you can see. Please, Mr. Nice said that there's nothing about Racak here. And what does it say here? Cafa Dulje, the 15th of January, 1989 [sic]. And then what does it say?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The combat position of the unit is unchanged, if I can see it right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's what written there, the combat disposition of the unit is unchanged. Could the units be engaged somewhere without the combat disposition being changed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's impossible because he'd give an order and then it would have to be written down here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm saying it is shown here, and how. When it says the combat disposition of the unit is unchanged, does that mean that the unit did not have anything except for its usual tasks?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The disposition is very important. The disposition remained the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the 16th the same thing. What is written there, the next page, number 2, the 16th. "Combat disposition --"

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unchanged, in number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I'm asking you, had they participated in anything, would it have to be written down here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have to write it down here. As I saw -- as I see on the next page, according to my order that I received from the corps commander, he was engaged and he wrote that down. He would have to write that down had there been any changes in the combat disposition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You explained on the map the deployment, and you mentioned the village of Kostanje and so on. Please. You said that one 30/2 was there.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One Praga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, one 30/2?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So one vehicle.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When that point was attacked, when fire was opened at it, what happened then? Do they take up their combat positions or do they remain sitting under tents?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The anti-aircraft units are the first ones to take up combat positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So are their combat positions marked here for months?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also since April, from the top of Canovica hill. So the green pine wood forest, one goes to Kostanje, and the other one goes down to the road that I showed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is their combat disposition every day?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one that was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that that's the one that was dug out, fortified, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For -- and how long were they there, prepared that way?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the month of April, when the entire unit went out there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from April 1998?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this handwritten material, the commander of the working group, it says unchanged on the 15th and on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the combat disposition of the unit remains unchanged. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not clear when the position in Kostanje was attacked. Were the troops in Kostanje position attacked ever? Do you mean on 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The positions at Kostanje elevation were never attacked. The positions were not in a village, they were on a hill. These were positions for anti-aircraft weapons. They have to be viewed individually, because in the report it says that the unit took up positions at Canovica hill, elevation -- you can't see it here. It's 700 and something -- overlooking Stimlje, about a kilometre and a half a way. And there's one at Kostanjevo, and the next one is at a point near the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. This unit was attacked then?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This unit was attacked and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then they took up their combat disposition?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the reason they did that was because they were attacked?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to preserve their men and their equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they had to disperse to previously established positions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, previously established positions and precisely defined tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I clarify one thing in terms of the language. While the other witnesses and the accused are saying "Kostanje," but, General, you are saying "Kostanjevo." Are you referring to the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same, but this is a hill. On the map it's very hard to distinguish these two points because it's such a small-scale map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you are saying "Kostanjevo" it means "Kostanje hill."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kostanje is 691. I found it here now, although it's not clearly visible. It's to the south-east of Stimlje, parallel to the road going to Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look now at this conversation of the 4th of February, 1999, shown to you yesterday by Mr. Nice. Brigadier General Maisonneuve and his associates conducted an interview with you, and I see that Colonel Kotur, who was the chief liaison officer of the corps, was also present. He was your liaison officer and so on. Let me just check what you said and what took place there, because Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 78, but it's also part of Racak binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll try and find a copy to place on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They can put the English on the ELMO to see if what I'm reading is correct. General, in several places here, and when General Maisonneuve testified, he also said that you didn't want to see him and then he made Kotur convince you, but we'll skip over that. And you say here on page 2 of his minutes - so these are his notes, not yours - that's him quoting you: "[In English] Regarding delaying the meeting, we have our daily tasks training soldiers."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "You have come many times unannounced ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Try again, Mr. Milosevic. Are you hearing now, General? Are you hearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you is that what you said to him, more or less? In connection with postponing the meeting, you had your regular duties in the army, and that he had arrived unannounced. "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... through liaison officer. You asked several questions, most answered by (K) --" [Interpretation] That's probably Kotur. I assume that's Kotur. "[In English] I wouldn't like to add to his answers but can if required. I do as directed for duty and to save the lives of soldiers. I'm very sorry, but that is the case here. I'm sorry you are focused on the results not the cause here. Unit at Stimlje was training and was fired upon. During the summer we lost three soldiers there marching in column. We were fired upon from 500 to 600 metres. I claim that no soldier hit any target closer than 500 metres."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is: Did he say this and what it's about. "It is incredible you say these things." That's what he says. And before that, he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're asking him to confirm whether he actually said those things?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, what is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There are several questions here. First of all, about the meeting I would like to say that this meeting was unannounced on the 16th. It was with the liaison officer. That was the usual form of communication with the OSCE, through the liaison officer from our units and through the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the question: Did you actually say those things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are several questions here. There are things I didn't say here as they are written down, but I have to analyse this document first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, what of the -- of the statements read by Mr. Milosevic, tell us which ones you did not say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that I didn't want to meet him and that I was forced by Colonel Kotur. On the contrary. At the next meeting that was scheduled, I had to delay it because I was out on the ground and the situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... pass over that and get on to the issue itself. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, what did you say was incredible of the things that he said? What was incredible? I'm not reading it out on purpose. Do you remember what the incredible thing was that he said to you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the details, but it's incredible that the army entered and did what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll read what he said. On page 1 here, he says: "[In English] - on the 15th of January my forces saw VJ tanks firing on houses with civilians who were not firing back."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you asking him whether that was one of the incredible things?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's what I'm asking him. It's the only thing that's said here. Maisonneuve says this before that. I wanted to hear what the incredible thing was that he said, and the general answered very well; he said the army wasn't there. That's why it's incredible. So he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's move on. We have covered that point then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on to say: "[In English] VJ did not conduct this operation but were in a position to defend themselves from their own position."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "[In English] So you surrounded village while the MUP operated in the village. Maybe the interpretation is not good. The military defended its position. If you were in Racak, you could see that the hills and mountains with trees are not good for tanks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the question now, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct? Is that what was said at the meeting, and did you tell him what you're testifying about now?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I didn't understand the interpretation. Not your interpretation here but the interpretation at the meeting. It was quite incredible what was said. Then he said that we were on the hills, but if you look at the topography, not a single combat vehicle could have even reached that area, not even in the summer let alone in the winter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he goes on to ask you, because you said only between Racak and Belince, he says you did not give support to the MUP operation, and you said no.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 16th of January, a day after the operation, and you said what you said here: "We had a meeting in Pristina headquarters."

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a planning meeting in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you said here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was absent that day because I was attending the meeting in the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In tab 19, there is an order issued by you which, according to Mr. Nice, is something we have already seen, so we won't dwell on it, simply an aspect of this. That's what you understood because that's how it was interpreted. My question is: Is this an order pertaining to the 26th of March, or is it a standing order beginning on the 26th of March?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander can issue a new order rendering null and void the previous order. This order entering into force on the 26th of March is a standing order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all I'm interested in. So it's a standing order until a new order is issued.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until a new order is issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So for how long was this brigade [as interpreted] acted upon in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 90 per cent of this was until the end of the war. A part referred only to part of the units which later came as reinforcements, after mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a few more questions. Did you ever receive an order from anyone apart from your immediate superior commander, that is the commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's well defined in all the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the rules. I'm asking you did you receive any such orders?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one else could have issued an order to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, just tell me, what in military terminology does the word "destruction of terrorist groups" mean, "cleansing the terrain of terrorists," and similar expressions? I want to know whether that means their physical destruction, their killing, or breaking down their military strength and eliminating them as a source of danger in the military sense. What in military terminology does "destruction of terrorist groups, and "cleansing the terrain of terrorist groups" mean?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our rules, these are rules for the lower levels of command, and it refers to companies, battalions, and units and artillery battalions which fight terrorist groups in certain areas and regions. You said this mentions destruction, imprisoning, and so on. "Destruction" means that unless an enemy unit surrenders, it should be destroyed. If they surrender, if they put aside their weapons, then they undergo criminal prosecution under the law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about "cleansing of the terrain"? Have you answered that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that it's cleansing of remaining terrorist groups. You can find this in battalion rules, artillery battalion rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've finished with my examination, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Kwon has one question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Jelic, you said to us that Colonel Petrovic, Pero Petrovic, had shown you a copy of his record after he had a meeting with Mr. Maisonneuve on the 16th of January, and you alluded to the possibility that we can find that record right now. Is it true? Do you think we can find the -- we can see the document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cannot give you a complete reply. After every meeting - that's what I said, if I recall - minutes were drawn up and a report compiled. The liaison officer, Mr. Petrovic, read this to me and then he registered it in the documentation and sent it on to the superior command, and this was sent at the time it was happening. It had to be done on the same day for operational purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If that document exists today, where do you think we can find it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order regulates that all documents, workbooks, targeting logs, lists, literally all documents had to be handed over to the command of the Pristina Corps in the Pristina garrison. That's where they all had to be handed over. I don't know what happened to them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, I'm very much interested in seeing this document, so I would encourage either party, the Prosecutor or the associate of the accused, to locate this document as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for attending at the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will take the adjournment now for 20 minutes, and then we'll move into the session where we'll hear submissions on the question that I have identified, and we'll start with the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the question raised by His Honour Judge Kwon, if you'll give us leave to rely on His Honour Judge Kwon's observations in a request to the authorities, we'll see if that works, rather than a formal order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. You have our authorisation to do that. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as indicated before, we're going to hear submissions on the question of extension of the time allocated to you for the presentation of your Defence. Do you have any submissions? Fifteen minutes for each party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was on. Thank you, Mr. Robinson. I am not going to use up the kindly allotted 15 minutes. I need much less time than that. I just want to remind you of Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights speaks in paragraph 3 of the minimum rights, and in subparagraph (b) it says to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence, inter alia. And (e) "[In English] to examine or have examined the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him." [Interpretation] There is no need for me to quote Article 6 of the European Convention on the Protection of Human Rights, because it says the same thing. I just want to remind you of the fact that Mr. Kay last time familiarised you with that enormous number of documents. He mentioned a figure of 1.200.000 pages. May I remind you of the fact that I never had the time to read that. So my rights have seriously been impaired already. Although you and Mr. Kwon - I'm not going to say Mr. Bonomy because he wasn't here - but the two of you remember that Mr. May would always say to me that that would be looked into, and it never was, as you know. In the meantime, as you know, I have shortened my witness list down to a minimum, so now it is about 190 witnesses altogether, which is truly the smallest possible number I need to call. I think that for that I need about 380 hours, counting on two hours on average for the examination-in-chief. Of course, some will require a lot more time, others a lot less, so I think that that would be a fair average. So let me be quite specific: I'm asking you for another 380 hours of time for questioning witnesses. That's what I had to say. Nothing else to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, why do you say that your right to examine witnesses under the same conditions as witnesses against you has been infringed, if you have been given the same time in terms of actual working hours as the Prosecution, to present your Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First and foremost, Mr. Robinson, I quoted these two paragraphs from the International Covenant on the Civil and Political Rights cumulatively. It also refers to time for preparation, which was never given to me. Also, as far as the preparation of witnesses is concerned, I know full well that various witnesses who testified for the other side there spent weeks and weeks here in preparation. My preparation time is very limited and it is boiled town to an hour and a half on working days and several hours on days that you consider non-working days or, rather, that are non-working for you. So from that point of view, there is hardly a trace of equality of rights. And even as far as the actual number of hours is concerned, that's not right either. When I added up my hours and Mr. Nice's hours, out of the 300 days of the Prosecution case, there is 70 days lacking. That was certainly not used up by witnesses coming into the courtroom, walking out, taking the solemn declaration and so on. So all of it is rather questionable, I think I should put it that way. You have the same information available, you can look at it. If you add up all the hours and divide it by the number of working hours per day, you get somewhat less than 200 says. So I'm saying that I have the right to adequate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your claim that you have 70 days less you had mentioned before, and I did ask you to put that in writing. Do you have anything to substantiate that that you can present to us now? It's not consistent with our records.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you have the records of the hours that were spent during the first half time when the Prosecution witnesses were called. Those were the hours used by Mr. Nice and the hours used by me. When you add that up together, it is not 300 days, it's 200 something. So that's a document that you have available. The Registrar has it. There's no need for me to submit it to you. You have it. So you cannot say that you have not been informed. Secondly, the fact that Mr. Nice used a great many 92 bis witnesses has to be taken into account. I could not avail myself of that possibility at all because I had no time for preparation. That's impossible. So if you say, well, you have something made available to you and you don't give me any time for availing myself of that opportunity, then it boils down to nothing. So this is a distortion. And I'm saying I have the right to adequate time, and that is estimated in accordance with the objective needs to present the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that's not a candid submission. You have available to you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- to help you. You have assistance available to you, and you could have relied on that in relation to the preparation of 92 bis statements. Those are your submissions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, several times you've said that I'm privileged because I have a room, a telephone, and so on and so forth. I wish to remind you of the following: That I did not get any of that until last year when I was supposed to begin. Throughout the first period of 300 days, I had none of that. I couldn't even meet up with my associates more than once or twice a week, because the area for receiving visitors was restricted, and that was treated like any other visit although all of this was going on here. Secondly, if you're saying privilege, for the time being I'm the only one who is handling his own case and represents himself. I'm the only one. I heard that Mr. Seselj has the intention to do that, that he -- and I think that he will avail himself of that possibility, too, and I think that's possible. So this is no privilege. On the contrary. It was not made possible for me to prepare my Defence in normal circumstances. So all of that was substituted for by one room and one telephone when it was finally given to me. So there can be no mention of equality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can we take it that your position is to stubbornly refuse to modify or alter your way of proceeding? You will continue to refuse to use the facilities which are available to present evidence more speedily by refusing to use counsel, your associates, in a productive way to gather together the statements which could be presented? You will intend, can we take it, to continue as you have done so far, with this unrealistic attitude that representing yourself means that you're entitled to do absolutely everything in the biggest case imaginable single-handedly? That remains your position?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am not saying at all that I'm doing everything single-handedly. My associates gather documents. I cannot even get to documents, as you know. They look through these documents. They see what can be used. They have enormous problems in obtaining documents. They have a very big job in this regard. As for the questioning of witnesses, I don't know if somebody else would question them faster than I'm questioning them here, so it's not a question of me doing whatever comes to my mind. On the contrary. I just examine witnesses. Everybody has to use time to examine witnesses. The associates cannot do that instead of me or parallel to me. Aren't witnesses supposed to testify here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we've had many examples of witness's whose evidence could have been presented far more effectively in writing than it has been by the oral examination that's taken place. You are, in fact, prejudicing your own case in the way in which you present it because of your inability to present and focus on the important issues, and you should be aware of that, that there are facilities available of experienced lawyers who would be able to put material together for you. But I take it from your answer you will continue to refuse to invite them to do that on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I hope that you, like I, understand what my right to self-representation is. It is an effective right, not a declarative right. So if I represent myself, then I should effectively be in a position to use that right, not for you to suggest now that somebody else should represent me in order to shorten time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you want to say anything in addition to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I won't repeat his argument, Your Honours, I'll just add a few extra features that it occurs to me he could have prayed in aid on his own behalf. All the Defence teams find it very difficult, in relation to the resources they have available to them, to employ Rule 89(F) and Rule 92 bis as a procedure for the presentation of evidence. They don't have as wide a range of professional investigators or people capable of taking a statement in a professional way. Some of the statements that may, say, take 20 or 40 pages could involve some two, three, or four days' work of a lawyer, and all Defence teams at the Tribunal have found it very difficult to employ counsel in that way, and the support staff available to them isn't really of the standard capable of producing effectively such material for a trial. The Prosecution have a different allocation of resources and set-up, and they're more easily able to draw down staff who are able to devote such time and resources to the creation of such statements. Notwithstanding that, one appreciates that they are Rules and decisions of the Tribunal that are within the jurisprudence of the Tribunal and they have to be acknowledged as being there. The point that I would make is that it is harder on the Defence to say, "Well, you can use the same Rules as them," when the reality is that it is a procedure more suited to the Prosecution and their establishment than any Defence team. And whilst it may be there, it is more suited to them. It was a request for a change in the Rules that emanated from the Prosecution. The Defence have never backed that approach in relation to the Rules and jurisprudence, being aware of their own limitations. As I take it at this stage, we're dealing with the issue of not an extended case in relation to a severed indictment of just Kosovo alone but of the whole three indictments and the situation of the accused generally in relation to the indictments that he currently faces. Our concern for the three indictments has been, as I said in the argument in relation to severance, that he has sufficient time to be able to put an effective defence in place as he has asserted there is one in relation to the Croatia and Bosnia indictments, and he has sufficient time available for that. We have only, in the Defence case to date, largely - 85 per cent, 90 per cent of the time - concentrated on the Kosovo indictment. My concern is that he has sufficient time for Kosovo as well as sufficient time for Croatia and Bosnia. In relation to the overall time that is sought by the accused, I haven't had an opportunity to translate that into any days or temporal figure as to what it works out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's actually quite easy, because it's not a million miles away from the original allocation in the trial, which is it's taking roughly 18 months to present the evidence for the 360 hours that were allocated. So if he seeks another 380, it's roughly another year and a half and a bit more. But we already know that his estimates for leading evidence in chief are way out and often more than twice the length of time that he projects. So the prospects are that the suggestion he's making would involve evidence being led for three years longer than is anticipated at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour. I hadn't factored in the Prosecution element within that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm assuming that has to be factored into any evidence that's led. I mean, if it's led, it will be cross-examined no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think the history, and I have to concede that, shows that the Prosecution will take issue with virtually everything that is put forward by the Defence, so there's no scope here for narrowing of issues on any agreed basis. The -- the question of the fairness of the time allocated to him, in our submission, should be to enable him to present an effective Defence. The Trial Chamber doesn't have to consider the parties as being on an equality of strength, because that would not be appropriate, in my submission. We are dealing with unequal professional and resource allocations. No matter what the Prosecution say about their resources and claim this, that, and the other, it is apparent there is a vast body of technical expertise out there that is able to produce matters during proceedings and produce filings, research that is beyond the scope and resources of any Defence team. So there is an inequality in strength. That has to be taken into account in relation to time for the accused to present his Defence on the indictments, that that has to be factored in in meeting the challenge mounted against him. And I say that as a general matter. I don't know if I can assist you any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, may I just add a sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in relation to this slowness, please, I wish to remind you of the following, precisely this Article 14 of the International Covenant, paragraph 1, which I did not quote: "[In English] Everyone shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing." [Interpretation] Public. I'm doing that by questioning the witnesses in public, orally, and that is perfectly in line with the Rules as stipulated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not, Mr. Milosevic. It's a question of how you interpret it. You very well know that the right to a public hearing is not absolute and that it can be derogated from in the interests of protection of victims and witnesses, and our Statute does that. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the question of calculation, I think I'm probably broadly in agreement with the figures estimated by His Honour Judge Bonomy. The accused's calculation of two hours per witness is about a third of our average to date. It's probably about 6 hours per witness. Two hours per witness, I think, would make about 30 weeks for examination-in-chief, so his average to date would be about 90 weeks in examination-in-chief. And then if you put in 60 per cent for cross-examination, you achieve about three years. The Prosecution's position is that there should be no extension of time and that the accused hasn't put up any argument to justify one. The Chamber carefully calculated the amount of time that we used and has allocated the same amount of time to him and has been, from first to last, courteous in two ways in dealing with him. I mean courteous, of course, in the ordinary sense of manners, but courteous in the sense of respecting him as a man of intelligence, and that's been a very proper -- a very proper course to take. It's said to him, This is what you're doing, these will be the consequences of your doing what you're doing. Now, there is -- there is no reason to deviate from that line unless the Chamber takes the view that he has been incapable intellectually of receiving the advice and information you have so regularly been giving him about what he must do if he is to bring this trial to a safe and satisfactory conclusion on his own behalf. Now, he has steadfastly refused to listen to that advice. Often, as we can see, he actually looks away when procedural matters are raised, as if to say he has no interest in them. But the fact remains that this Chamber gave him always the best advice and told him what he had to do. Now, he not having done that and having, on any view of a professional lawyer, simply wasted his time, he's in no position to say what additional time he might have required had he acted sensibly and economically. Things might be different. If he'd acted -- done all he could to achieve a satisfactory result in the time allowed to him and then at the end of it said, "Well, look, I've done my best but I still need a bit more time," well, then, of course the Court could consider it and indeed it might be people wouldn't oppose it, but we simply have no idea what position he would have reached had he behaved in that sensible and logical way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is the problem I have with this, Mr. Nice, precisely. But can I ask you about these figures you gave. You're working on the basis of 190 witnesses, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think he said two hours examination-in-chief, so that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But just from what -- is it 190 witnesses; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But six hours for 190 witnesses, if that's what you estimate the time would be, will be roughly -- yes, 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About a thousand hours and a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then a thousand hours and a bit divided by four, 250 days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nearer 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nearer 300, so it's a huge amount of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And at three days a week over 40 weeks in the year, or whatever is actually achieved, I think it's a significantly longer period than -- I wasn't using that sort of calculation, but that comes to much longer than the period I was envisaging; a lot longer than the three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may well be. My arithmetic is very rapidly done. And, Your Honours, the -- one is bound to observe that since the Chamber's hearing a couple weeks ago on severance, there has been no reduction of time taken in examination by the accused or in re-examination save for one instance. Indeed, there has been clearly an extension or certainly a cleaving to the original practice if not an extension of it. I must mention the one exception. The Chamber will remember that, for whatever reason, there was a very settled determination that the witness Farkas should leave on a particular day, and there was a very efficient re-examination conducted of that witness, I think about 20 minutes, showing that this accused well knows how to deal with matters efficiently when he wishes to. So that it's our firm and respectful position that the Chamber must have the courage to stand by its decision which was made with the accused's interested in mind, which has been put into effect at all times respectful of his intelligence and of his ability, and that would simply reflect the fact that he has chosen to put himself into a corner or, in reality, to attempt to put the Chamber into a corner, and that is something that, of course, would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the accused has been given the same number of working hours as the Prosecution had in presenting its case. What would you say to the argument that equality in these circumstances doesn't necessarily add up to fairness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Nice's other microphone please be turned on because the booths have problems hearing him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same point I was making earlier, I think: We'll never know. It may well be that an accused doing his best to make use of the procedures available to him to present his case in a proper way to Court would come to the end of his case either shorter than the Prosecution took, and the Chamber would see that time is being wasted on unnecessary witnesses and would bring it to a close, or would exhaust the time and then say, "Please can I have some more," and be granted it. But there is nothing in the different services or resources available to one side or the other automatically to say that there is inequality. Now, Mr. Kay's arguments, I'll deal with just a couple of them, but his arguments that the Defence find it difficult to use 89(F) or 92 bis because counsel won't or can't do the work of preparing witness statements is something that simply can't affect this trial at this stage. The practice of using written evidence for examination-in-chief is widespread around the world and established for all civil cases in the United Kingdom, as an example, and has been for many years. The experience how to deal with it is therefore experience available to all. If the accused had decided to follow the Chamber's advice and indeed to emulate the Prosecution's practice once 89(F) was permitted as a method of saving time and he was finding it difficult because he had inadequate resources, why, he need only have drawn the matter to the Court's attention and no doubt something would have been done because this Court has been absolutely determined to ensure that when the accused wants something by way of resources, he gets it. So that I'm afraid that argument simply can't do. But it's very important to bear in mind that the argument about resources is a new development in the accused's armoury by which he confronts these proceedings. I drew to your attention - I can't remember how many weeks ago it was but it was only a few weeks ago - that this was a new part of what he was saying. Up until then it was not practical matter. He simply expressed an absolute determination to deny the advice he was receiving, to thwart the Chamber by saying, thank you very much, he would have everything in writing. Then suddenly, about -- I think probably about a month ago, maybe five weeks, we first heard some suggestion about the difficulties. It is -- there are no difficulties. We've seen him with his witnesses with sheets of points. Sometimes, when they've been looking at notes, knowing exactly what question is coming and what document's going to be dealt with. Of course it's within his capability, given that he must use associates and lawyers, so his proposition that he's got to do everything himself is fanciful. Of course it would be within his ability. After all, neither Mrs. Del Ponte nor I see every witness ourselves. She sees none. Of course I see some but not all of them before evidence is given. I prepare or supervise the preparation of witnesses, but I don't do it all myself. How could I? The proposition of the accused, if ever taken seriously, for a Tribunal like this would be, of course, to make its work completely impossible. And if he had wanted to, contrary to his absolute determination to call everything orally, he could have put in place a system for calling witnesses - 89(F) or 92 bis - a year and more ago, and he should have done that. Now, Your Honour, I'm not sure that that specifically deals with or sufficiently deals with Your Honour's point about inequality. As to the inequality of resources, yes, of course a Prosecution office, here as in any other jurisdiction, is likely to have immediately to hand more resources of certain kinds than will be available to a Defence lawyer, solicitor, or counsel. That may not make any form of inequality. At this stage of the trial, an accused is meeting allegations where the burden of proof is not on him. He meets those allegations by identifying witnesses to be called and then identifying the exhibits he wants those witnesses to produce. And we've seen with the last witness a striking example of inequality, on this occasion the inequality going the other way. It's clear that the last witness, Jelic, or, rather, the accused or his associates, so far as Jelic was concerned, had ready access to a range of documents that we've been trying to -- that's the orders in the file, that we've been trying to get hold of for three years. We've seen earlier examples of him being able to produce overnight war diaries when we've been trying to get them for years. So the inequalities are not always the same way, and indeed, though -- I won't say that. So inequality is in no way to be taken as an assumed reality. It may exist, but we don't know. It hasn't been established as something that requires more time, and even so, if there was any suggestion that it might establish, for some reason, more time, we simply don't know how much more time because of the way the accused has wasted the opportunities given him by this Court. Your Honours, the only basis upon which we could envisage that the Chamber might allow the accused more time than that presently allowed is if the Chamber, looking back, says to itself: "Well, we treated him as an intelligent person capable of responding to advice, applying his brain to the problems at hand, but we see we were wrong to do that. We should have treated him in some way as incapable or disabled." In the absence of making such a finding that he was simply incapable of responding to Court orders and advice given from the Bench, and no doubt advice available to him from my learned friends, then the proper course is to grant him no extension of time and to work on the basis, as I said in a recent pleading, that by pushing everyone, as he's been seeking to do, into a corner that will extend and delay the trial to unacceptable lengths, by doing that, he should in fact be treated as someone who has made a voluntary, informed, and intelligent decision to call no evidence beyond that or beyond the issues that he has covered by the time his time runs out. And if that means dealing with him as somebody who has made an informed decision to call no evidence for Croatia or no evidence for Bosnia, so be it. I should add, I think, this: If one looks back at the history of attempts to deal with various problems of delay in this case, when this Chamber decided to assign counsel, it was very careful to do so solely on the basis of health. Again, it showed the accused courtesy in making no other adverse findings against him. When the Appeals Chamber changed the order of modalities, which inevitably had an effect on the time that the accused's evidence would take, this Chamber respected that decision absolutely. And if it is to any extent the modalities order that leads to the present position, then the Chamber can be confident that reflecting and respecting that order is something that should find favour elsewhere, but that's a matter for another time and another place. The only other matter I might refer to is this: The volume of paper issue. It comes up time and again and is, I fear, a misrepresentation of reality, but I must deal with it. The volume of paper that has to be served on a person in the position of this accused is always going to be enormous given our duty to help him wherever we can with exculpatory material. It's a problem of a particular scale for a case like this but it's a major problem for all trials. It's a problem that it may be helpful if everyone knows this - by that I don't mean the Chamber but I mean the public as well - it's a problem that's been addressed by making to a greater extent or the greatest extent possible material available electronically so that people can search it themselves, but it -- it is not within our power to reduce the quantity of material it's our duty to make available to the accused save and insofar as the accused would agree to narrower parameters that we have identified as appropriate to search on his behalf. And I think uniquely to this Trial Chamber, from the beginning I set out our parameters and what we were doing on searching, and I asked the parties to -- not the parties, I asked all others in court, including the Bench, to make observations if they had reservations about the way we were searching it, and save for one increase in breadth of parameters, stimulated, I think, by a discussion with Mr. Kay, nothing else has come. So there's nothing that can be done, and of course the vast majority -- not the vast majority, a very large amount of the paper that's been served on the accused has been repeat serving done by Ms. Dicklich, frequently unasked, simply to make it clear that -- make it possible for the accused to have material related to a particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the things that's been done to help this accused is that Ms. Dicklich has always repeated service of material on him before witnesses were called in order to save him having to go and search for it. He knows that. We also know that he uses the Rule 68 disclosure material, and efficiently, in drawing it out in examination of his own witnesses and earlier in cross-examination of ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm reminded that - this is in paragraph 13 of our recent filing - in February of this year it was His Honour Judge Robinson who cautioned the accused that he shouldn't expect leniency or accommodation on account of matters relating to time when he didn't authorise the services which was -- which were available to him, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That should have been "utilise," I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is an absolute unreality on the part of the accused which would lead to the trial either never ending or almost never ending, and that may be what he wants, and it has to be resisted. The Chamber has acted - I repeat this - with consummate fairness and courtesy in all broad senses of that word to the accused and his intelligence and the time has come when the Chamber should say to him: "No more. You will bring this case to a conclusion on the time we allowed you."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, do you have anything to say on the recent medical reports? These reports have been passed on to you, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was delivered to Mr. Rakic. Maybe. But I have not seen any reports in the last few days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How could that be? Mr. Legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, have you received these reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've had a copy from the ear expert, is how I described it in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the 6 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's also a report from Dr. van Dijkman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which date is Your Honour talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 2nd, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can't comprehend, Mr. Milosevic, the circumstances in which you would not have received these reports.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- is 6th of December, 2005, from the ear expert, which we received on the 7th, and I wasn't had any other in December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have one from the neuroradiologist?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've got Dr. Dijkman's of the 1st of December. That's the first, yes. But no others last -- this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you've said you got one dated the 6th, which is Dr. -- that's Dr. Delarts [phoen]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Delarts is on the 29th of November, and then there's the other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Delarts largely confirmed what Professor Andric said, I think, about the hearing problem and the nature of it, and the other reports were more connected with whether there's a link between that and the cardiovascular difficulties, and I think the one from the neuroradiologist deals with the six points that are made by Dr. Shumilina, and there is also one that suggests a method of coping. Dr. Dalal, I think, coping with the hearing difficulties Mr. Milosevic experiences in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That was the technical one, which contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you've got everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, we've got all those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, just clarify, have you received the neuroradiologist's report, Dr. Aart?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Aart?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's the 6th of December. That happens not to be in this file. That is waiting to be filed and is in the pile in the other room, but yes, that's the one that we received on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I can't understand why the accused would not have received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've had it. Dr. Rakic -- sorry, I shouldn't call him Dr. Rakic. Professor Rakic is certainly here and would have received it; he's on the mailing list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We'll make sure that a copy is provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the submission that you made for another 380 hours would work out to something in the region of another three years' extension of the case. Can you tell me why, if that is so, it would not be reasonable for me to assume that you did not make that submission seriously and responsibly and why should I not be in a position to assume that it reflects a cynical disregard for the duty of this Court to ensure a fair and expeditious conclusion of these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, first of all, I cannot understand how you transformed 380 hours into three years. That means you're counting on a hundred hours a year. It's probably a problem with your intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Nice worked it out. It is for you to say why it should not amount to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in my efforts to shorten as much as possible all necessary times and the list of witnesses, I have reduced this to 380 hours.
