As you know, that's not so much. It must be clear to you how long 380 hours is. I'm pointing out the fact that 380 hours are calculated on the basis of two hours per witness on the average. I want you to know that not for a moment have I tried to prolong the time. On the contrary, I've been trying to make the most rational use of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Bear in mind that your actual use of time is about twice your estimated time. That's borne out by what has actually happened. That's not a matter of guessing, of conjecture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's another matter. These estimates of the time required have not always been correct, I have to say. Sometimes a witness requires more time, more questions. There are more responses. Various other circumstances arise which slow down the examination. However, I am calculating on the efficient use of this time. Every working day here has four hours and 15 minutes. Let's say it's only four hours. Therefore, 380 hours is less than a hundred working days, much less. How Mr. Nice turned this into three years is something I fail to understand. Four hundred hours would amount to a hundred working days. But this is less. Ninety, let's say, or something on those lines. You can't say it's a year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You haven't included cross-examination, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If that's 90, then with cross-examination it would be 150. That's 150 days. It's not a year let alone three years. Some elementary mathematics are in question here. It's not higher mathematics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This concludes the hearing. Let the witness Sel be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before the witness comes in, can I raise a procedural matter concerning him but in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fear I shan't be able to conclude the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subject to the way that our propositions are dealt with, I would have thought it take a session, and although that will -- it would extend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would hope so but we'll see how he deals with the points that I raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, Mr. Sel. Sit, be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you remain under the declaration that you made. Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, you will recall that questioning of you, based on propositions coming to the Prosecution from two men who had spoken to investigators, giving the names Colovic, led to your identifying the existence of diaries. Those diaries were ordered to be produced to the Court, and they were provided. They're handwritten diaries. We have only photocopies of them. The originals have been retained in Belgrade. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've had a certain limited number of pages translated in part only, very small parts. The bundles that I will distribute, if I may, have the translated pages at the beginning and the limited number of pages that have been translated in part following, this to accord with the Chamber's practice for such documents of not producing as an exhibit anything other than is referred to in court. We have a full version for the witness to look at because he may wish to satisfy himself that what he sees is complete. The page numbers of both diaries -- or pages of both diaries are numbered, although the numbers are often faint and sometimes illegibly faint. The Chamber will see, if it casts its eyes to the back of the selection it has, that the pages have been photocopied in open-page format so that you can see frequently one or both numbers. I'm looking at 67, 68, 69 -- 68 and 69, for example, where the numbers are clearly seen. And at the beginning, the Court has the same page numbering used. The Court may be content in the first stages, and for speed, simply to go to the pages in English being referred to the original pages, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sel, have you looked at the -- can you just have a look at the full copy, please. This is not going to be produced as an exhibit, but it's available for you to refer to. This has been provided from Belgrade, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the army. Just look at it and satisfy yourself that this would appear to be a copy of your two diaries, please.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I would like to correct you on this point. This is not a diary. This is not a diary. This is a work notebook. I as company commander did not keep a diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. It's a notebook. Is it your notebook?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's my notebook. It's from the period of 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to run through pages as quickly as I can by topic, and the first topic, which I'd like to deal with very swiftly, is your saying on the last occasion you knew nothing of either an Ersad or a Semso Colovic. Would you please go to page 33, bottom right-hand corner. And on the right-hand page, immediately under the entry for the 25th of June, 1998, do you see the name --

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I don't have that page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll make sure that the pages are brought to you directly. After 33, it will be --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation said another number and I see in the transcript that Nice said 33. It must have been a misinterpretation because the interpretation said 43 and that's why the witness cannot find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] Page 33, Mr. Sel, and the date 25/06/98.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your hand, is it, the reference in search of Colovic?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, it is written in my hand. Colovic Ersad - let me just explain - was permitted to go on medical leave to be examined by a doctor. It was on the 15th or 16th of June that we got up there and he was allowed to go to the military hospital in Nis to be examined by a doctor. He did not report to the military hospital in Nis and since then he was seen in the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You remembered nothing about Colovic on the last occasion. What is it that has stimulated your memory on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is 1998. Without notes -- I mean, that's what I said, I would like to have my own notes, my work notebook, so that I could check things out so that it wouldn't seem that I were not telling the truth or something like that. So I did have Ersad Colovic, who was a young soldier, the 1998 generation -- just a moment, let me finish. He was transferred to my unit around the 15th of June. He was allowed to leave camp to go to see a doctor on account of his illness, but then from then on he never reported back to the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, on the last occasion you knew nothing about Colovic. We can't decipher everything on the page that you've been looking at, the single first page of the diary, but just tell us, can you read there this account of his going to a hospital and then being -- and not returning? We can only read "In search of Colovic." It doesn't say anything about going to a hospital.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, on the camp premises we had no doctors, so the soldier was taken down to Djakovica, along with an escort, to be examined by a physician. That is the main reason -- that is the main reason why soldiers went to barracks --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- from the camping premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked why it was you couldn't remember anything about this person the last time and now you can remember all this detail when the only thing in the book is the name. Now, do you understand that question, first of all? And if you understand it, would you please try to answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I understand the question very well but it seems that you don't understand me. On the basis of the note I have here, I remembered the soldier. Without the notes -- I told you very nicely during my last testimony, without notes I cannot confirm whether this is correct or not. That's why I ordered, on the 25th of June, 1998, that the search for Colovic start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that, having seen this name, you remembered everything. That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not just the name, it's what is written here. It's "In search of Colovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we go on to -- I don't want to trouble you with this, but page 37, please, just to complete this exercise of four entries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 37 you will see, on the left-hand side of you, you'll see a further reference to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 36, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It hasn't, I think, been translated but it doesn't matter. You can see, I think -- and this has only just been identified by me, we can add it in -- you can see on the left of page 36 another entry, "Still looking for Colovic." Yes? Can you see that there, middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Nice. What it says here Colovic, Ersad. We received a report that he's in hospital, and it says "Hospital." That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just read out the entry. Is it in your hand?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Colovic." I cannot see the name now. Then it says "Hospital." Sorry, no. I'm sorry, he was wanted at that time. An APB was issued because he left of his own free will. He was on the run, and that's why he became a wanted person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we go to the next page, which is at 56 for you, we see his name again in a list of names of people. Number 2 on the list: Ersad Colovic.

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says up here, Mr. Nice, it says "Fugitive." So he is a fugitive. He's on the run. Legally, an APB was issued through the security organs or, rather, through the relevant services. So from then onwards he was no longer in the unit. That is 1998, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 68, please. You see, what I want to know, Mr. Sel, where you may have answered the point already, is -- just one moment. We'll move on to -- don't worry about 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can't go beyond 1.43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go on, then, to page -- no, not 35. 170, I think. If it's not there I'll ask the question I want to ask in any event. No, don't worry about 170. It's not there. For the time being, it doesn't matter. We've already seen three references, and there may be two or three others, to Colovic Ersad. When I put allegations to you that I told you had come from the mouth of Ersad Colovic last time, you completely denied his existence in your unit. Is that because you knew that this man was likely to be able to tell the truth about you?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's been a long time. If you listen to me carefully and if you understood me, I said very nicely that without my work notebooks I cannot establish whether that soldier was in my unit or not. So in fact from the 20th of June, 1998, this soldier was a fugitive. And how can he make a statement about me from 1999 when he was not in the unit at that time at all?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Develop, with one question, His Honour Judge Kwon's point. Is your brain one where you see a single word, like "Colovic," there is -- even though you'd heard the word, seeing the word on the page stimulates the whole recollection of events surrounding him? Is that what happens with your brain?

utterances.speaker: JANOS SEL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let's not go into how everybody's brain functions. I said that I needed notebooks in order to see whether that soldier was in my unit or not. As you can see, this soldier came to my unit around the 15th of June, but on the 20th of June, 1998, he himself became a fugitive from the unit. From then onwards, he was a fugitive. So as for any statements that he could give about me, they could only pertain to training in camp. In that period of time, the unit did not take part in any kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I just want to note it's not the single word "Colovic." There were three or four "In search of Colovic," and that might have triggered --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I didn't think there was any reference in there to the hospital or anything else, but Your Honour, I see that I have my work cut out to finish in the time allotted, if the answers are going to be similar, on the next week.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I was saying was, Mr. Robinson, there is a phenomenon called visual memory. So isn't it normal that a witness may remember things once he's seen his notebook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a comment you can make at another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll see how he does with other words next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are going to adjourn, Mr. Sel. You will have to return -- you will have to return on Monday at 9.00 a.m. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 12th day of December, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
